document.title: East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. submits Request for Rehearing of the 09/29/2026 Order
document.group: Rehearing of FERC's PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement order

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
 
) 
EL26-108-00 
 
 
) 
 
REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF 
EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC. 
 
Pursuant to section 313 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Rule 713 of the 
Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,2 East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. 
(“EKPC”) respectfully requests rehearing of the Commission’s order accepting, subject to refund 
and additional proceedings, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) revisions to its Open Access 
Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities 
(“RAA”) establishing the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) .3 
The Commission erred in accepting aspects of the RBP Proposal without adequately 
addressing EKPC’s cost-causation objections. The Commission did not explain why the existing 
self-supply portfolio of a load-serving entity (“LSE”) may be disregarded in determining the LSE’s 
RBP exposure, or why qualifying offsets need not reduce the obligations of the LSE or the load 
that supplied them. Nor did it explain whether it accepted PJM’s default allocation to all LSEs in 
a zone/area when no state- or Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”)-
determined allocation is reported or reserved that distinct issue for further proceedings. The 
Commission rejected EKPC’s Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) comparability argument 
without adequately addressing the relevance of comparable resource-planning actions by 
 
1 16 U.S.C. § 825l (2018). 
2 18 C.F.R. § 385.713 (2026). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,245 (2026) (“Order”).

2 
Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) self-supply LSEs. And, despite setting certain collateral 
elements for paper hearing, the Commission did not adequately address EKPC’s foundational 
objections to the exposure, quantity, release, and default-allocation methodology underlying the 
LSE collateral requirement. 
Although the Commission established paper hearing procedures on cost allocation, 
Transmission Owner exit rules, and LSE collateral requirements, it stated that aside from the issues 
reserved for hearing, “the other aspects of PJM’s RBP proposal are just and reasonable.”4 The 
Order does not clearly establish whether the independent cost-causation and collateral-
methodology objections identified below remain open. To the extent that the Commission rejected 
those objections or accepted the challenged provisions, EKPC requests rehearing. Alternatively, 
EKPC requests clarification that the paper hearing encompasses those objections and that no 
adverse determination has been made on them. A subsequent section 205 proposal does not resolve 
whether the Order adequately addressed the framework before the Commission. 
I. 
Background 
A. 
RBP Proposal 
PJM filed the RBP Proposal on July 31, 2026 as a one-time procurement of new capacity 
for terms of up to 15 years, beginning no earlier than the 2028/2029 Delivery Year and ending no 
later than the 2042/2043 Delivery Year.5 At the zone/area level, PJM proposed to allocate the 
Initial RBP Target to Electric Distributor zone/areas based on each zone/area’s pro rata share of 
the difference in forecasted Load Adjustments between the 2026/2027 and 2028/2029 Delivery 
Years, reduced by qualifying offset capacity and opted-out load, and to fix that allocation for the 
 
4 Order at PP 23-24. 
5 Order at PP 1, 15.

3 
15-year term.6 At the LSE level, within each zone/area, PJM proposed to allocate costs to LSEs 
based on a state- or RERRA-determined RBP Obligation (“RBO”) reported by the Electric 
Distributor. If no RBOs are reported, PJM would allocate the zone/area’s RBP Charges to all load 
in the zone/area using each LSE’s ratio share of the Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation under 
RAA, Schedule 8.7 Separately, PJM proposed an LSE collateral requirement equal to an RBP 
Credit Rate of $1.5 million multiplied by committed RBP MW, payable in cash or letter of credit 
45 days before the first Delivery Year, with defaulted RBP Charges reallocated to remaining 
LSEs.8 
B. 
Protest 
EKPC timely intervened and filed a Protest, supported by the Affidavits of Adam 
Bednarczyk and Carl F. Coscia, Ph.D. on August 21, 2026.9 EKPC also filed a Limited Answer 
on September 4, 2026,10 and a Second Limited Answer, supported by a Reply Affidavit of Dr. 
Coscia, on September 18, 2026.11 The Commission accepted EKPC’s Answers.12 
In proposing the RBP, PJM claimed that the RBP is “a critical safety net designed to 
address current resource adequacy shortfalls.”13 EKPC shares PJM’s concern about resource 
 
6 Order at P 99 (citing Proposed Tariff, attach. DD, § 18.3(a)). 
7 Order at P 110 (citing Proposed Tariff, attach. DD, § 18.3(b)). 
8 Order at PP 183-84 (citing Proposed Tariff, attach. DD, §§ 18.8, 18.9). 
9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., “Protest of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.,” Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (filed 
Aug. 21, 2026) (“Protest”); Affidavit of Adam Bednarczyk, Attachment 1 to Protest (“Bednarczyk Affidavit”); 
Affidavit of Carl F. Coscia, Attachment 2 to Protest (“Coscia Protest Affidavit”). 
10 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Motion for Leave to File Limited Answer, and Limited 
Answer, of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.” (filed Sept. 4, 2026) (“EKPC September 4 Answer”). 
11 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Motion for Leave to File Limited Answer, and Limited 
Answer, of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.” (filed Sept. 18, 2026) (“EKPC September 18 Answer”); Reply 
Affidavit of Carl F. Coscia, Attachment 1 to EKPC September 18 Answer (“Coscia Reply Affidavit”). 
12 Order at P 22. 
13 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource 
Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads” (filed July 31, 2026) (“PJM RBP Filing”).

4 
adequacy and the reliability challenges facing the PJM region. Fundamentally, however, as EKPC 
explained in its Protest,14 the RBP is inconsistent with the Commission’s cost-causation principles. 
EKPC has argued and demonstrated, with record evidence, that the RBP fails to “protect LSEs 
whose existing resource portfolios already support their expected load obligations from incurring 
additional costs.”15 That risk extends to entities like EKPC “whose supply portfolio contains 
sufficient resources to serve the load underlying PJM’s forecast.”16 
As EKPC explained in its Protest, to be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory 
or preferential, rates must reflect the cost-causation principle that “all approved rates reflect to 
some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them.”17 In its Protest, EKPC 
explained that rate design decisions must be supported by “substantial evidence.”18 PJM failed to 
provide any evidence “that allocating costs based on total zonal load obligations bears any 
reasonable relationship to the load growth that caused the shortfall. LSEs with no or minimal large 
load growth may nonetheless be allocated disproportionate costs due to improper accounting of 
the offsets and opt-outs or the use of the default allocation methodology.”19 The potential for 
socializing costs across all LSEs, regardless of causation, fails the legal and economic tests of “just 
and reasonable” ratemaking.

15 Protest at 11. 
16 Protest at 11. 
17 Protest at 30 (quoting KN Energy, Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992)). 
18 Protest at 21 (citing Elec. Consumers Res. Council v. FERC, 407 F.3d 1232, 1233 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (“Upon applying 
the usual APA standard, we conclude that the Commission’s approval of the rate design is supported by substantial 
evidence in the record and is not otherwise arbitrary and capricious.”)). 
19 Protest at 21.

5 
The evidence provided by EKPC in the Bednarczyk Affidavit shows that a generalized 
showing of regional reliability need does not support PJM’s particular rate design.20 As explained 
by Mr. Bednarczyk, the RBP does not “track mitigation measures” or keep costs aligned with the 
parties who create or mitigate the need.21 Existing resources cannot earn RBP revenue, and treating 
them differently becomes a problem when the Tariff also refuses to count them in deciding who 
caused the need.22 For self-supply LSEs like EKPC, the question is whether their own resource-
adequacy actions reduce their RBP exposure.23 As Mr. Bednarczyk explained, self-supply LSEs 
face particular risk if their resource positions are not recognized,24 and crediting offsets only at the 
zonal level weakens incentives for forward procurement.25 And regarding PJM’s proposed default 
cost allocation, by defaulting to Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation, PJM is defaulting to a “broad 
capacity-allocation metric” that “does not identify the LSEs that created the residual procurement 
need.”26 Under the proposed default allocation methodology, an LSE whose load growth is 
ordinary and whose resources are sufficient bears costs caused by another LSE.27 As explained by 
Dr. Coscia, unlike Peak Load Contribution (“PLC”)-based charges, which follow measured load, 
the RBP Obligation assigns a fixed 15-year quantity based on a forecast that does not fall if the

21 Bednarczyk Affidavit at P 7. 
22 Bednarczyk Affidavit at PP 25-26. 
23 Bednarczyk Affidavit at P 35.

27 Bednarczyk Affidavit at P 18.

6 
load never appears.28 The Load Adjustment inputs were submitted for planning purposes and were 
never verified for cost allocation.29 
Dr. Coscia’s Affidavits also addressed the exposure basis and quantity underlying the credit 
and collateral requirements, the interaction with existing PJM credit rules, and the treatment of 
defaults.30 Proposed Tariff Attachment DD section 18.9(a) requires reallocation of defaulted RBP 
Charges among remaining LSEs responsible for those charges, while application of the defaulting 
LSE’s collateral is permissive.31 Dr. Coscia’s Affidavits separately identify potential residual 
exposure under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 for Members without an initial RBP 
allocation.32 That concern does not depend on EKPC receiving a zero allocation: it concerns the 
relationship between the exposure secured, the entities posting collateral, and the entities 
potentially bearing a residual loss.33 
As explained by EKPC in its Protest and Answers, EKPC recognizes the urgency of PJM’s 
reliability concerns.34 But the RBP as accepted fails to achieve its objectives in a manner consistent 
with the requirements of the FPA. The RBP assigns long-term costs and collateral obligations 
through a framework that lacks the specificity necessary to be just and reasonable because the RBP 
does not sufficiently identify the LSE responsible for causing the capacity shortage, does not 
ensure that any offsets or opt-outs follow the entity that secured them, and does not protect LSEs 
whose existing resource portfolios already support their expected load obligations from incurring 
 
28 Coscia Protest Affidavit at PP 159-61. 
29 Coscia Protest Affidavit at PP 159-61. 
30 See Coscia Reply Affidavit at PP 18-24, 71-73. 
31 See Proposed Tariff, attach. DD, § 18.9(a); Coscia Reply Affidavit at PP 18-24. 
32 See Coscia Protest Affidavit at PP 168-70; Coscia Reply Affidavit at PP 18-24. 
33 See Coscia Reply Affidavit at PP 21-24. 
34 Protest at 10-11. See also EKPC September 18 Answer at 3-4.

7 
additional costs. The RBP may attempt to address a legitimate reliability need. But simply 
attempting to address a legitimate need is not enough to make the RBP Proposal just and 
reasonable, especially where the resulting costs are not reasonably tied to cost causation. 
C. 
The Commission’s Order Accepting the RBP Proposal Subject to 
Additional Proceedings 
In the Order, the Commission accepted the RBP for filing, suspended it for five months to 
become effective February 28, 2027, subject to refund, and established paper hearing procedures 
and an FPA section 206 proceeding in Docket No. EL26-108-000.35 The Commission identified 
three hearing topics: cost allocation, Transmission Owner exit rules, and LSE collateral 
requirements.36 It stated that “the other aspects of PJM’s RBP proposal are just and reasonable.”37 
On cost allocation, the Commission questioned reliance on Load Adjustments, directed briefing 
on updated load forecast information, and “decline[d] to further address arguments raised in the 
protests related to PJM’s proposed cost allocation method at this time.”38 It separately upheld the 
FRR exclusion and rejected the comparability argument concerning RPM self-supply LSEs.39 On 
collateral, it upheld seller collateral, questioned LSE collateral, and expressly requested responses 
on “(1) what initial RBP Credit Rate is appropriate and (2) whether 45 days before the start of the 
delivery year is sufficient time for LSEs to post collateral.”40 Those questions do not clearly 
establish the treatment of the independent allocation and collateral-methodology objections raised 
here. 
 
35 Order at PP 1, 23-27. 
36 Order at P 24. 
37 Order at P 23. 
38 Order at PP 154-60. 
39 Order at P 151. 
40 Order at PP 203-06.

8 
The Commission set forth the correct standard by which it must evaluate PJM’s method 
for allocating RBP costs, explaining that “[u]nder the cost causation principle, all Commission-
jurisdictional rates and charges must ‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the 
customer who must pay for them,’”41 and that “costs must be allocated in a manner that is at least 
roughly commensurate with benefits.”42 The Commission explained that it “may approve a given 
cost allocation framework if it ‘has an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits 
are at least roughly commensurate with’ the assigned costs.”43 Although the Commission 
articulated that standard and reserved aspects of cost allocation for further proceedings, it did not 
clearly explain the treatment of EKPC’s distinct LSE-level objections concerning portfolio 
recognition, offset attribution, and the default allocation. Instead, the Commission addressed the 
applicability of the RBP to FRR Entities, stated that aspects of PJM’s RBP Proposal may not be 
just and reasonable, and set a limited number of issues for additional proceedings.44 The 
Commission failed to address several of the central cost-causation concerns raised by EKPC. 
II. 
Statement of Issues and Specification of Errors 
Pursuant to Rules 713(c)(1) and (2), and 203(a)(7),45 EKPC provides the following 
statement of issues and specification of errors: 
1. 
The Commission erred by failing to address EKPC’s argument that a self-supply 
LSE’s existing portfolio of resources must be considered. This failure is arbitrary, 
capricious, not the product of reasoned decision making, and contrary to law. 5 
U.S.C. § 706(2). See, e.g., Env’t Def. Fund v. FERC, 2 F.4th 953, 967-68 (D.C. Cir. 
2021) (“Thus, the overarching question in this case is whether ‘the Commission’s 
decisionmaking [wa]s reasoned, principled, and based upon the record.’”) (citation 
 
41 Order at P 150 (quoting KN Energy Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992); see also Ky. Pub. Serv. 
Comm’n v. Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp., 193 FERC ¶ 61,110 (2025) (Ky. Comm’n)). 
42 Order at P 150. 
43 Order at P 150 (quoting Ill. Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 477 (7th Cir. 2009)). 
44 Order at PP 2, 150-51. 
45 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.713(c)(1), 385.713(c)(2), 385.203(a)(7) (2026).

9 
omitted); NBCUniversal Media, LLC v. NLRB, 815 F.3d 821, 823 (D.C. Cir. 2016) 
(“NBCUniversal”) (“When an agency’s decision lacks adequate justification 
because it is neither logical nor rational, or because it fails to offer a coherent 
explanation of agency precedent, the judgment under review is wanting for lack of 
reasoned decisionmaking.”). 
2. 
The Commission erred by failing to address EKPC’s distinct argument that PJM’s 
treatment of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW reduces the aggregate procurement 
target without requiring the offset to reduce the RBO MW, RBP Charges, or 
collateral obligation of the LSE or load that supplied or sponsored it. To the extent 
the Commission accepted that treatment, its failure to explain the resulting 
allocation is arbitrary and capricious and contrary to cost-causation principles. 
Alternatively, the Commission failed to clarify that LSE-specific offset attribution 
remains within the paper hearing. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). See, e.g., Env’t Def. Fund v. 
FERC, 2 F.4th 953, 967-68 (D.C. Cir. 2021); New England Power Generators 
Ass’n, Inc. v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202, 211 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“It is well established that 
the Commission must respond meaningfully to the arguments raised before it.”) 
(quoting TransCanada Power Mktg., Ltd. v. FERC, 811 F.3d 1, 12 (D.C. Cir. 
2015)). 
3. 
The Commission erred by accepting the challenged cost-allocation features without 
adequately applying its cost-causation principles or, alternatively, by failing to 
clarify that those issues remain open for paper hearing. In particular, to the extent 
the Order accepted the default allocation among LSEs, it did so without explaining 
its consistency with cost causation. The Commission’s failure to provide a reasoned 
explanation is arbitrary, capricious, not the product of reasoned decision making, 
and contrary to law. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). See, e.g., N.Y. & Atl. Ry. Co. v. Surface 
Transp. Bd., 635 F.3d 66, 71 (2d Cir. 2011) (“Surface Transp.”) (“An agency also 
acts in an arbitrary and capricious manner if the ‘agency departs from its own 
precedent without a reasoned explanation.’”) (citation omitted); Greater Boston 
Television Corp. v. FCC, 444 F.2d 841, 851-53 (D.C. Cir. 1970) (“Greater 
Boston”) (“An agency’s view of what is in the public interest may change. . . . But 
an agency changing its course must supply a reasoned analysis indicating that prior 
policies and standards are being deliberately changed, not casually ignored.”) 
(citations omitted); FPL Energy Marcus Hook, L.P. v. FERC, 430 F.3d 441, 448 
(D.C. Cir. 2005) (“FPL Energy”) (“[W]e can only uphold the Commission’s 
interpretation if we can ‘discern a reasoned path’ to the decision.”); NBCUniversal, 
815 F.3d at 823 (D.C. Cir. 2016) (“When an agency’s decision lacks adequate 
justification because it is neither logical nor rational, or because it fails to offer a 
coherent explanation of agency precedent, the judgment under review is wanting 
for lack of reasoned decisionmaking.”); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of the United 
States v. State Farm Mut. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (“Motor Vehicles”) 
(“[A]n agency rule would be arbitrary and capricious if the agency . . . offered an 
explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency[.]”). 
4. 
The Commission failed to engage in reasoned decision making to the extent it 
accepted, or excluded from further examination, the challenged LSE collateral

10 
methodology without addressing EKPC’s objections concerning the exposure 
secured, applicable MW quantity, interaction with Attachment Q and Peak Market 
Activity, reduction and release standards, application of collateral before default 
reallocation, and potential residual exposure under Operating Agreement section 
15.2.2. Alternatively, the Commission failed to clarify that those issues remain open 
for paper hearing. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). See, e.g., Surface Transp., 635 F.3d at 71 (“An 
agency also acts in an arbitrary and capricious manner if the ‘agency departs from 
its own precedent without a reasoned explanation.’”) (citation omitted); Greater 
Boston, 444 F.2d 841 at 851-53 (“An agency’s view of what is in the public interest 
may change. . . . But an agency changing its course must supply a reasoned analysis 
indicating that prior policies and standards are being deliberately changed, not 
casually ignored.”) (citations omitted); FPL Energy, 430 F.3d at 448 (“[W]e can 
only uphold the Commission’s interpretation if we can ‘discern a reasoned path’ to 
the decision.”); NBCUniversal, 815 F.3d at 823 (“When an agency’s decision lacks 
adequate justification because it is neither logical nor rational, or because it fails to 
offer a coherent explanation of agency precedent, the judgment under review is 
wanting for lack of reasoned decisionmaking.”); Motor Vehicles, 463 U.S. at 43 
(“[A]n agency rule would be arbitrary and capricious if the agency . . . offered an 
explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency[.]”). 
5. 
The Commission erred in its determination that there is no undue discrimination 
between FRR Entities and RPM LSEs. This determination is arbitrary, capricious, 
and not the product of reasoned decision making. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). See, e.g., Env’t 
Def. Fund v. FERC, 2 F.4th 953, 967-68 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (“Thus, the overarching 
question in this case is whether ‘the Commission’s decisionmaking [wa]s reasoned, 
principled, and based upon the record.’”) (citation omitted); Pacific Gas & Elec. 
Co. v. FERC, 306 F.3d 1112, 1115, 1121 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (noting that Commission 
“must be able to demonstrate that it has made a reasoned decision based upon 
substantial evidence in the record” and remanding case because reviewed orders 
“provided no explanation as to how or why” the Commission’s conclusion 
produced necessary outcome); NBCUniversal, 815 F.3d at 823 (“When an agency’s 
decision lacks adequate justification because it is neither logical nor rational, or 
because it fails to offer a coherent explanation of agency precedent, the judgment 
under review is wanting for lack of reasoned decisionmaking.”). 
6. 
The Commission erred by failing to meaningfully consider the evidence provided 
in the Bednarczyk and Coscia affidavits. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). See, e.g., 
Sithe/Independence Power Partners, L.P. v. FERC, 165 F.3d 944, 948 (D.C. Cir. 
1999) (“The Commission must be able to demonstrate that it has made a reasoned 
decision based upon substantial evidence in the record, and the path of its reasoning 
must be clear.” (quoting Town of Norwood v. FERC, 962 F.2d 20, 22 (D.C. Cir. 
1992) (internal citations and quotations omitted))); Williston Basin Interstate 
Pipeline Co. v. FERC, 358 F.3d 45, 48 (D.C. Cir. 2004) (The Commission must 
make a “reasoned decision based upon substantial evidence in the record.”); Motor 
Vehicles, 463 U.S. at 43 (agency decision is arbitrary and capricious if “offer[s] an 
explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before [it]”); S.C. Pub. 
Serv. Auth. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41, 54 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (The Commission’s findings

11 
must be supported by substantial evidence, which means “such relevant evidence 
as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.”); BNP 
Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d 264, 270 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (“[W]e 
cannot affirm on the basis of a Commission rationale that fails to respond to critical 
arguments raised before the agency.”); New England Power Generators Ass’n, Inc. 
v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202, 211 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“It is well established that the 
Commission must respond meaningfully to the arguments raised before it.”) 
(quoting TransCanada Power Mktg., Ltd. v. FERC, 811 F.3d 1, 12 (D.C. Cir. 
2015)). 
III. Request for Rehearing 
Under the Administrative Procedure Act and federal appellate court precedent, the 
Commission’s decisions will be set aside on appeal if they are “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of 
discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law,” or “unsupported by substantial evidence.”46 
For the Commission to have engaged in reasoned decision-making, it must have examined the 
relevant data and provided a rational connection between the facts found and the choices made.47 
If the Commission “does not provide a rational explanation for its action based on relevant data, 
then that action is arbitrary and capricious.”48 Here, EKPC, a party aggrieved by the Commission’s 
Order,49 seeks rehearing of the Order because it is arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion, 
not based upon substantial evidence in the record, and otherwise contrary to law. 
The FPA’s just-and-reasonable standard incorporates the cost-causation principle, under 
which all approved rates must “reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer 
who must pay them,” and costs must be allocated in a manner at least roughly commensurate with 
 
46 5 U.S.C. §§ 706(2)(A), 706(2)(E). See also Vistra Corp. v. FERC, 80 F.4th 302, 312 (D.C. Cir. 2023); S.C. Pub. 
Serv. Auth. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41, 55 (D.C. Cir. 2014); Sacramento Mun. Util. Dist. v. FERC, 616 F.3d 520, 528 (D.C. 
Cir. 2010). 
47 Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. Motor Vehicles Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983). 
48 La. PSC. v. FERC, 20 F.4th 1, 6-7 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (citing 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) and Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n, 
463 U.S. at 43)). 
49 See 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a) (party aggrieved by order of Commission may seek rehearing). See also Order at PP 20-22 
(noting Joint Protestors’ respective interventions and consequent party status in this proceeding).

12 
benefits.50 The Commission must have an “articulable and plausible reason to believe that the 
benefits are at least roughly commensurate with” the assigned costs.51 Undue discrimination occurs 
where similarly situated customers are treated differently without adequate justification.52 Finally, 
a filed rate must possess the minimum specificity that the Commission can reasonably require, 
such that customers can determine who is responsible for a charge and in what amount.53 
A. 
The Commission Erred by Failing to Address EKPC’s Argument That 
It Is Unjust and Unreasonable for the RBP to Ignore a Self-Supply 
LSE’s Existing Portfolio. 
In its Protest and Answers, EKPC argued that the RBP should consider a self-supply LSE’s 
existing portfolio in determining the LSE’s RBP obligations. The Commission failed to address 
this argument. That failure was arbitrary and capricious, not the product of reasoned decision 
making, and contrary to law. 
As EKPC explained in its Protest, the RBP fails to account for existing resources in an 
LSE’s supply portfolio. The relevant question in evaluating the RBP under the Commission’s cost-
causation principle is whether the entity assigned costs as a result of the RBP caused the resource 
adequacy shortfall that the RBP is intended to address and/or whether it benefits from the 
procurement and associated allocated costs.54 An LSE whose self-supply portfolio fully covers its 
load, including any incremental large load, has not contributed to the resource adequacy gap on 
that showing.55 Any broader regional benefit does not, without further explanation, justify the 
 
50 KN Energy, 968 F.2d at 1300; Ill. Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476-77 (7th Cir. 2009); Old Dominion 
Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1260 (D.C. Cir. 2018). See also Order at P 150. 
51 Ill. Com. Comm’n, 576 F.3d at 477. 
52 TranSource, 168 FERC ¶ 61,119 at P 240. 
53 Pub. Utils. Comm’n of Cal. v. FERC, 254 F.3d 250, 255 (D.C. Cir. 2001); Protest at 18-19. 
54 See Protest at 11-12. 
55 Protest at 11-14; 45-47; Bednarczyk Affidavit at PP 25, 31, 61-63.

13 
particular RBP costs assigned to that LSE. The Commission did not explain why cost causation 
does not require PJM to credit a self-supply LSE’s resource position against that LSE’s own RBO, 
RBP Charges, and collateral requirements. 
This issue is not clearly resolved by the paper hearing questions concerning updated 
zone/area load forecasts.56 Correcting the measurement of load growth does not itself determine 
how an existing self-supply position affects an LSE’s responsibility in the first instance. To the 
extent that the Order accepted this feature, the Commission must address EKPC’s objections on 
rehearing. If it intended to reserve it, then the Commission should expressly confirm that the 
hearing encompasses existing portfolio recognition. 
The Commission’s failure to respond to EKPC’s significant, record-supported objections, 
and its reliance on distinctions that do not address the cost-causation question presented, is 
arbitrary and capricious and not the product of reasoned decision-making.57 Accepting a rate 
design that may require a self-supply LSE to pay for RBP capacity that provides it little or no 
additional reliability benefit is inconsistent with the requirement that costs be at least roughly 
commensurate with benefits.58 This outcome also weakens the incentives that the RBP is intended 
to promote and is in tension with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge’s objective of ensuring that new 
large loads, not prudently planning LSEs and their existing customers, bear the costs of new 
capacity.59 
 
56 See Order at PP 157, 159-60. 
57 Motor Vehicles, 463 U.S. at 43; PPL Wallingford Energy LLC v. FERC, 419 F.3d 1194, 1198 (D.C. Cir. 2005). 
58 Ill. Com. Comm’n, 576 F.3d at 477; Bednarczyk Affidavit at P 34. 
59 See EKPC September 18 Answer at 9-10; Bednarczyk Affidavit at PP 34, 38; Order at P 161.

14 
Section 205 of the FPA requires that “all rules and regulations affecting or pertaining to” 
rates and charges subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission “shall be just and reasonable.”60 
Courts have consistently required the Commission to use reasoned, principled decision-making in 
determining whether rates are just and reasonable. Courts have explained that the Commission 
must “adequately explain how the evidence it relied on ‘support[ed] the conclusion it reached.’”61
